terms.meaning: A substance that shows different colours in acidic and basic solutions.
Turns blue litmus red. Usually tastes sour.
Turns red litmus blue. Usually tastes bitter and feels soapy.
Neither acidic nor basic. It changes neither red nor blue litmus.
A fungus and an alga living together on rocks and trees. Litmus is extracted from it.
A substance whose smell changes in an acidic or basic medium.
The reaction in which an acid and a base cancel each other out.

items.name: Litmus test
items.formula: Acid: blue → red. Base: red → blue. Neutral: no change in either.
items.example: Lemon juice turns blue litmus red. Soap solution turns red litmus blue. Sugar solution changes neither.

items.name: Red rose extract
items.formula: Acid: a shade of red. Base: a shade of green.
items.example: Vinegar makes the extract red. Baking soda solution makes it green.

items.name: Turmeric
items.formula: Base: yellow → red. Acid and neutral: stays yellow.
items.example: A yellow curry stain turns red when washed with soap.

items.name: Other plant indicators
items.formula: Extracts of many coloured plant parts also act as indicators.
items.example: Beetroot, purple cabbage, jamun and red hibiscus.

items.name: Onion as a smell test
items.formula: A cloth kept with onion keeps its smell in acid and loses it in base.
items.example: Useful for a person who cannot see the colour change.

items.name: Hydrangea flowers
items.formula: Flower colour shows the soil: blue in acidic soil, pink or red in basic soil.
items.example: The same plant can change colour when moved to different soil.

items.name: Lemon and orange
items.example: Both taste sour because of this acid.

items.name: Tamarind
items.example: Tamarind water turns blue litmus red.

items.name: Curd
items.example: Curd tastes sour while milk does not. Page 11 asks you to find this one out.

items.name: Vinegar
items.example: Vinegar turns blue litmus red. Page 11 asks you to find this one out.

items.name: Amla
items.formula: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and citric acid
items.example: A sour fruit that is also rich in vitamin C.

items.name: Tomato
items.example: A tomato tastes sour because of these acids.

items.name: Red ant bite
items.example: The acid in the bite causes the stinging pain.

items.name: The neutralisation reaction
items.example: Mix lemon juice and lime water in the right amount: the mixture is neither acidic nor basic, and it warms up.

items.name: Lime water
items.formula: A solution of calcium hydroxide, made by mixing lime (chuna) in water and filtering.
items.example: It is basic. It has nothing to do with the lime fruit.

items.name: Treating an ant bite
items.formula: Rub on a mild base to neutralise the acid.
items.example: Moist baking soda on a red ant bite.

items.name: Treating soil
items.formula: Too acidic: add lime. Too basic: add organic matter such as manure.
items.example: A farmer uses lime on soil made acidic by too much chemical fertiliser.

items.name: Treating factory waste
items.formula: Add basic substances to acidic waste before it reaches a lake or river.
items.example: This protects the fish in the lake.

items.name: Father of modern Indian chemistry
items.formula: Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray, who founded Bengal Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals.
items.example: He also wrote on the history of chemistry in India.

mistakes.text: Turmeric staying yellow does not prove a solution is acidic. It stays yellow in neutral solutions too.
Not everything bitter is a base. Bitter gourd tastes bitter but is not basic.
Lime water comes from chuna, not from lime fruit. Lime water is basic, while lime fruit is acidic.
Never taste an unknown substance to test it. Use an indicator.
